source: USDA ARS Fruit Lab / University of Maryland Extension Mid-Atlantic Commercial Strawberry IPM Program
title: Strawberry Anthracnose Fruit Rot and Crown Rot (Colletotrichum acutatum, C. gloeosporioides, C. fragariae)
content: Strawberry anthracnose is the most economically important and destructive fruit rot, crown rot, and foliar disease complex of cultivated strawberry (Fragaria x ananassa Duchesne ex Rozier, family Rosaceae) worldwide in warm, humid, subtropical and temperate production regions. It is caused by three closely related species of hemibiotrophic ascomycete fungi in the genus Colletotrichum (class Sordariomycetes, order Glomerellales, family Glomerellaceae; teleomorphic Glomerella sexual stages, now synonymized under Colletotrichum): (1) Colletotrichum acutatum J.H. Simmonds species complex (Group A2; includes C. nymphaeae, C. fioriniae, C. simmondsii, C. salicis, C. godetiae; the most widely distributed and most important causal species on strawberry fruit in North America, South America, Europe, Australia, and New Zealand - responsible for 85-95% of all strawberry anthracnose fruit infections); (2) Colletotrichum gloeosporioides (Penz.) Penz. & Sacc. species complex (Group A1; includes C. fructicola, C. theobromicola, C. siamense, C. aenigma - primarily causes anthracnose crown rot in warm subtropical nurseries, Florida winter plug production, and California central coast strawberries; can also cause fruit rot); (3) Colletotrichum fragariae A.N. Brooks (Group A3; primarily causes foliar leaf spot, petiole lesions, and runner blight in the southeastern United States and parts of South Africa; rarely infects fruit and crowns in the field). The strawberry anthracnose complex occurs in all major strawberry-growing regions of the Americas (United States: California, Florida, Oregon, Washington, North Carolina, Maryland, New York; Canada: Quebec, Ontario, Nova Scotia; Mexico, Guatemala, Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, Brazil), Europe (Spain, France, Italy, Germany, Poland, United Kingdom), North Africa, the Middle East, South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Korea, and China. Annual production and economic losses from strawberry anthracnose are conservatively estimated at 300-500 million USD globally (2023 figures); fruit rot epidemics can destroy 50-80% of an entire strawberry field's harvestable crop within 1-2 weeks of warm rainy weather during the fruiting period. Transplanted crown rot infections from contaminated nursery stock can cause 10-40% plant mortality within 6-10 weeks of transplanting, requiring costly replanting. The most economically damaging and commonly observed symptom of strawberry anthracnose (specifically, C. acutatum / C. nymphaeae) is anthracnose fruit rot (AFR) on green, white-pink, and ripe red strawberry fruit. On ripening and ripe fruit, the first visible lesions are small (1-3 mm), circular, slightly sunken, soft, water-soaked, light brown to tan spots that expand rapidly (within 24-48 hours under warm humid conditions) into larger, dark brown to black, firm, sunken, circular to irregular lesions 5-30 mm in diameter. Under humid conditions (RH > 90%, dew, or light rain), the surface of mature fruit lesions develops characteristic diagnostic masses of abundant, gelatinous, pink-to-salmon-colored, slimy conidial spore masses (called 'acervular exudate' or 'spore tendrils') composed of millions of single-celled, hyaline, falcate (crescent-shaped, fusiform) C. acutatum conidia (12-24 x 3.5-5.5 um, tapered to a point at both ends) oozing from dark, setose (bearing black bristle-like setae), acervular fruiting bodies embedded just below the fruit cuticle. These slimy salmon-pink spore masses are the key diagnostic feature distinguishing anthracnose fruit rot from the other major strawberry fruit rots: Botrytis gray mold (gray fuzzy sporulation), Rhizopus leak (coarse whiskery black sporangia), Sclerotinia white mold (white cottony mycelium + black sclerotia), and Phytophthora leather rot (brown firm leathery lesions with distinct greenish margins + no surface sporulation). Infected ripe fruit loses firmness rapidly, develops an unpleasant bitter flavor from mycotoxin accumulation (colletotrichins, C16/C18 cyclic depsipeptides, and beauvericin; regulated in EU, Japan, and Australia under food safety maximum limits), becomes completely unmarketable both for fresh retail sale and for processing (frozen, jam, puree), and often mummifies on the strawberry plant if not harvested. On immature (green) strawberry fruit, C. acutatum produces small (1-5 mm), firm, hard, dark brown to black, slightly sunken, 'dry-rotted' lesions; green fruit lesions are often quiescent (latent, symptomless) and resume active necrotrophic expansion only as the fruit begins to ripen (color change from green to white to pink/red) at approximately 7-10 days before harvest. This latent/quiescent infection mechanism explains why strawberries that appear completely healthy at harvest can develop devastating anthracnose fruit rot after 3-5 days in cold storage or during transit to market - a major source of post-harvest economic loss for strawberry shippers. In addition to fruit rot, C. acutatum also causes anthracnose lesions on strawberry flower petals (anthracnose blossom blight, resulting in failure to set fruit), tiny black 'sprig' lesions on runners and pedicels (fruit stalks), and irregular, small, dark brown to black leaf spot lesions on the upper surfaces of strawberry leaflets. The second important syndrome is anthracnose crown rot (ACR), caused most frequently by C. gloeosporioides / C. fructicola and some pathogenic C. acutatum isolates: initially, the youngest emerging strawberry trifoliate leaves and central bud (crown meristem) wilt, turn flaccid, and develop a dull bluish-green or reddish-purple discoloration, often on only one side of the plant (one-sided wilt, a highly diagnostic symptom distinguishing ACR from Phytophthora crown rot which usually causes uniform whole-plant wilting). Within 3-7 days after the first wilt symptom, the entire strawberry plant collapses, turns brown, and dies; when the diseased crown is cut open longitudinally, firm, firm-textured, reddish-brown to brownish-black marbled necrotic areas and streaks are visible within the crown cortex and vascular tissue (in contrast to Phytophthora fragariae var. rubi red stele root rot, which produces a characteristic reddish discoloration strictly in the central stele vascular cylinder of the main root). The third syndrome is anthracnose leaf spot / runner blight, caused primarily by C. fragariae in the southeastern US: 3-10 mm circular to irregular dark brown necrotic spots on leaflets, and elongated, sunken, dark brown to black girdling lesions on runners that often kill the unrooted daughter plant at the end of the runner. All three Colletotrichum species are disseminated primarily via symptomless infected strawberry nursery planting stock (dormant bare-root crowns, plug transplants, and runner tips); the pathogens survive internally as latent, quiescent, hemibiotrophic mycelium in the epidermal, cortical, and vascular tissues of apparently healthy strawberry crowns, runners, petioles, flower buds, and the calyx (cap) tissue of immature green fruit. This is the primary mechanism of long-distance, international, and regional spread of strawberry anthracnose: a single symptomless plug plant from an infested nursery can introduce the pathogen into a clean production field and serve as the initial focus of a devastating local epidemic. Within a local production field, secondary polycyclic spread of C. acutatum and C. gloeosporioides conidia occurs EXCLUSIVELY via splash dispersal of the sticky, gelatinous, salmon-pink conidial masses from acervuli on infected fruit and plant tissues by raindrops and overhead sprinkler irrigation water; the sticky, mucilaginous matrix surrounding Colletotrichum conidia prevents wind dispersal over long distances, so within-field secondary spread is limited to splash distances of approximately 1-3 meters from an infected source plant. Conidia germinate and penetrate host tissues directly through the cuticle via melanized appressoria (24-48 hours post-deposition) or through small natural openings and wounds (insect feeding punctures, hail damage, mechanical abrasion from harvest operations). Infection and fruit lesion development are optimum at temperatures of 25-30 C (77-86 F) and require minimum 4-6 hours of continuous free surface moisture on fruit from rain, dew, or overhead irrigation; the latent period (infection to first visible fruit lesion with sporulation) is only 3-5 days on ripe fruit at optimum temperatures. C. acutatum can survive in soil and on the surface of strawberry polyethylene mulch for up to 9-12 months as thick-walled, melanized chlamydospores and microsclerotia, and as saprotrophic mycelium colonizing dead strawberry crop residue (leaves, petioles, crowns, old roots); it does not require a living strawberry host for short-term persistence. Management of the strawberry anthracnose complex is one of the most challenging tasks in commercial strawberry production worldwide; an integrated multi-component program is mandatory. (1) EXCLUSION via certified disease-free nursery planting stock is the single most important management practice. Use ONLY strawberry transplants (bare-root dormant crowns, plug trays, and runner tips) that are officially certified by an established national government or university strawberry certification program with mandatory annual field and greenhouse inspections and mandatory random-sample laboratory PCR / qPCR testing for Colletotrichum spp. (examples of reputable programs: USDA-APHIS Strawberry Certification Program in the US, the California Strawberry Certification Scheme CSCS, the British Columbia Berry Council Certification Scheme in Canada, the NPTC Strawberry Certification Scheme in the UK, the CTIFL certification in France, the HAL Pflanzenbescheinigung in Germany, and the AusBerry Certification Scheme in Australia). In the US, avoid uncertified 'Florida winter plug' transplants from general-market sources that have not been tested for C. gloeosporioides crown rot, as these historically have been the source of major anthracnose crown rot outbreaks in the mid-Atlantic and northeastern US. (2) Genetic resistance is the most economically effective long-term strategy. Strawberry anthracnose resistance is quantitatively inherited, polygenic, and species-specific: multiple different QTLs and FaRC (Fragaria Resistance to Colletotrichum) loci control resistance to C. acutatum (fruit rot) vs. C. gloeosporioides (crown rot). No modern commercial strawberry cultivar is completely immune to anthracnose; however, the following commercially important cultivars carry moderate to high levels of quantitative partial resistance to C. acutatum fruit rot in university field trials (NC State, UMD, Cornell, USDA ARS Beltsville): 'Chandler' (high resistance to fruit rot, susceptible to crown rot), 'Flavorfest' (very high fruit rot resistance), 'Allstar' (moderate resistance), 'Jewel' (moderate), 'Camarosa' (high fruit rot resistance), 'Albion' (day-neutral; moderate), 'San Andreas' (day-neutral; moderate to high), 'Monterey' (day-neutral; moderate), 'Portola' (day-neutral; moderate), 'Winter Dawn' (short-day Florida; moderate). C. gloeosporioides crown rot resistant cultivars include 'Sweet Charlie', 'Treasure', 'Bish', and 'Pelican'. (3) Cultural practices: (a) use raised, plastic-mulched beds (black, white-on-black, or virtually impermeable film VIF) with drip tape under-mulch irrigation; NEVER use overhead sprinkler irrigation for fruiting strawberry fields because overhead water is the sole splash-dispersal mechanism for C. acutatum secondary spread. (b) plant strawberries into fields that have been rotated out of strawberry and other Rosaceous fruit crops (raspberry, blackberry, peach, apple) for 3-4 years; avoid fields with a documented previous history of severe anthracnose crown rot. (c) for annual hill / plasticulture production systems in the mid-Atlantic and southeastern US, pre-plant soil fumigation with approved soil fumigants (chloropicrin, 1,3-D, metam sodium, metam potassium, allyl isothiocyanate) reduces soil-borne C. acutatum chlamydospore populations by 60-90%; Telone C-35 (1,3-D + chloropicrin 65:35) and Pic-Clor 60 (chloropicrin 60% + 1,3-D 39%) are the most effective fumigant combinations against both crown rot and fruit rot inoculum. For non-fumigated organic production systems, 3-4 weeks of pre-plant anaerobic soil disinfestation (ASD) using rice bran or molasses as carbon source at 20 t/ha reduces soil inoculum levels by 50-70%. (d) remove and destroy (burn, landfill, hot-compost) all infected fruit (both mummies on the plant and fallen fruit on the mulch surface) and any wilted dead plants showing crown rot symptoms at least weekly during the fruiting season; do NOT compost anthracnose-infected material on the farm because C. acutatum chlamydospores survive standard cool composting temperatures. (e) use 60-gram weight low-tunnel quick-hoop low tunnels covered with 5-mil greenhouse plastic during the main fruiting period to keep rain off fruit; this simple practice can reduce anthracnose fruit rot incidence by 70-85% even without fungicides, as it completely eliminates splash dispersal. (f) for pick-your-own operations, provide hand-sanitizing stations for customers, and instruct pickers not to handle obviously rotted fruit to prevent mechanical spread of inoculum. (g) post-harvest handling: cool harvested strawberries to 34-36 F (1-2 C) as quickly as possible (within 30-45 minutes of harvest) using forced-air pressure cooling to slow post-harvest expansion of latent anthracnose infections; do not mist or wet fruit after harvest; maintain strictly controlled cold chain during storage and shipment. A 2-minute post-harvest dip in 50-65 C (122-149 F) hot water + 25% hydrogen peroxide (food-grade, 0.5% v/v) or 1% potassium sorbate reduces post-harvest anthracnose development by 40-60% with acceptable fruit quality retention. (4) Chemical fungicide programs for conventional commercial strawberry production: begin protectant fungicide sprays at the early bloom stage (10% open flowers) and continue on 7-14 day intervals through final harvest, depending on rainfall and temperature. The most effective FRAC groups against the Colletotrichum anthracnose complex (based on 2019-2024 UMD, NC State, Cornell, USDA Beltsville, and UCANR trial data): FRAC 11 QoI / strobilurins (azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin, trifloxystrobin, picoxystrobin; excellent protectant + good translaminar movement; however, C. acutatum QoI-resistant populations carrying the Cyt b G143A mutation have been widespread in Florida, California, Maryland, North Carolina, and Spain since 2013-2015, so QoIs must ALWAYS be alternated and tank-mixed with multi-site partners and limited to 4-5 applications maximum per season). FRAC 7 SDHI (fluxapyroxad, boscalid, isofetamid, pydiflumetofen, penthiopyrad, benzovindiflupyr; excellent protectant + mild systemic curative activity; FRAC 7 + FRAC 11 premixes are the industry-standard conventional backbone). FRAC 3 DMI triazoles (metconazole, tebuconazole, difenoconazole, prothioconazole, tetraconazole, myclobutanil; good protectant + limited 2-day kickback activity against blossom and green-fruit latent infections; rotate with other groups). FRAC M3 multi-site (mancozeb, maneb, metiram, captan; excellent zero-resistance-risk contact protectant; mandatory tank-mix partner for all single-site fungicides; captan is particularly effective against fruit surface inoculum when applied 1-2 days before rain events). FRAC M1 copper hydroxide (Bordeaux mixture, copper oxychloride, tribasic copper sulfate; moderate protectant activity; permitted in organic programs under NOP standards). FRAC 9+12 anilino-pyrimidine + phenylpyrrole (cyprodinil + fludioxonil; Switch 62.5WG; excellent protectant + kickback activity; one of the most effective single products for anthracnose fruit rot control ever developed). FRAC 40 + 40 (mandipropamid + cyazofamid; ineffective against anthracnose - use only for downy mildews, do not use against Colletotrichum). Strict FRAC anti-resistance management rules: (i) always tank-mix every single-site fungicide application with a full labeled rate of FRAC M3 captan or mancozeb. (ii) maximum 2 consecutive sprays of the same FRAC group, then switch to a different group. (iii) limit FRAC 11 QoI, FRAC 7 SDHI, and FRAC 9+12 to 4-5 total seasonal applications maximum. (iv) end the spray program with a multi-site contact protectant (captan, mancozeb) to minimize selection pressure for resistance in the final crop of inoculum surviving to the next season. (5) Organic strawberry production anthracnose management programs rely on: (i) certified resistant or partially resistant cultivars; (ii) rain-excluding low tunnels; (iii) strict overhead irrigation bans; (iv) weekly fruit sanitation (roguing of all infected fruit); (v) 7-10 day rotational sprays of fixed copper, wettable sulfur, lime sulfur (dormant only), Bacillus amyloliquefaciens QST 713 (Serenade ASO / Serenade Opti), B. subtilis GB03 (Kodiak), Pseudomonas chlororaphis strain AFS009 (Howler), Streptomyces lydicus WYEC 108 (Actinovate AG), Trichoderma asperellum T11 / T. harzianum T-22 (RootShield Plus PLUS), Reynoutria sachalinensis (Regalia Maxx) extract, orange oil (Citrex, Prev-Am Ultra), and hydrogen peroxide + peroxyacetic acid (Oxidate 5.0, Jet-Ag); organic programs on susceptible cultivars typically achieve 40-70% reduction in anthracnose fruit rot compared to untreated under moderate disease pressure. (6) Post-harvest biological control: experimental treatments with the yeast antagonist Metschnikowia fructicola NRRL Y-27328 (formerly Candida oleophila strain O, commercialized as Aspire) and the Gram-negative bacterium Pantoea agglomerans CPA-2 applied as post-harvest dip treatments at 10^8 cfu/mL reduce post-harvest anthracnose expansion by 55-75% on stored fruit and are registered for post-harvest use on strawberries in the EU, Canada, and Israel, with US EPA registration pending as of 2024.
